opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that, at the frontier, research and training are really the same activity seen from two angles. Many of the most important research questions only show up when you train at scale. An idea that looks great on a small model can disappear or even backfire on a big one, and some problems, like training instabilities, loss spikes, or odd interactions between data and architecture, simply don't exist at small scale. If the research team works in its own sandbox and hands results over a wall, a lot of that knowledge gets lost in translation.

It also goes the other way. The people running large training jobs build up a very concrete, almost tactile sense of what's happening: which data mixtures behave strangely, where the optimization gets fragile, what the infrastructure can actually support. That intuition is research insight. If they're treated as "just executing" someone else's plan, you waste the best source of new ideas you have.

Then there's speed. For a company like ours, the advantage doesn't come from having more people or more compute than everyone else. It comes from iterating faster. Every handoff between teams adds latency: you write documents, you schedule syncs, you argue about whose priority wins. When the same group owns the hypothesis, the experiment, and the production run, the loop from "I have an idea" to "I know whether it works at scale" gets much shorter.

And finally, it's about ownership and taste. A model isn't a sum of independent modules you can optimize separately. Architecture, data, optimizer, and infrastructure are all coupled. You need people who carry the whole picture in their heads and feel responsible for the final model, not just their piece of it. Splitting research and training tends to create local optima, where each team does well by its own metric but the model as a whole doesn't get better. So we try to keep them tightly integrated, even though it's messier organizationally.

r001.rationale: The response says important problems emerge during large-scale training and that training experience provides research insight. It does not state that solving a problem encountered in training requires having understood it beforehand.

fable-5.1.text:
Because in large models, research and training are not really two different activities. They are the same activity viewed at different moments.

When people talk about separating research from training, the mental model is usually borrowed from traditional software or from older machine learning. Someone has an idea, they validate it at small scale, they write it up, and then an engineering team takes it and runs it on the production system. That works when the idea transfers cleanly across scales. In large models it often does not. A trick that gives you a nice gain at one billion parameters can disappear, or even reverse, at a hundred billion. Data mixtures that look optimal in a small ablation behave differently once the model becomes capable enough to actually use the data. So if the people who had the idea are not the same people watching the big run, they never see the evidence that tells them whether the idea was right.

The other issue is that most of the real insight comes out of the training process itself. You look at loss curves, you look at how the model behaves at different checkpoints, you notice something strange and you go investigate. That is research. But it happens inside training. If you draw an organizational wall there, the people with the research intuition are not in the room when the interesting things happen, and the people in the room are not set up to ask why.

There is also a question of feedback loops. Large runs are expensive and slow. You cannot afford to run many of them. So each one has to carry as many hypotheses as possible, and you need people who can read the results and immediately decide what to change for the next one. If that decision has to go through a handoff between two teams, each with its own priorities and its own understanding of the system, you lose both speed and information. The context that matters is often informal, things like "we tried this variant two months ago and it looked fine at small scale but we were never sure." That kind of knowledge does not survive a document.

So in practice I think of it as one team that moves along a spectrum. Some people spend more time on small-scale experiments and some spend more time on infrastructure and large runs, but everyone is responsible for the same question, which is whether the final model gets better. Once you make the model the shared object rather than the paper or the pipeline, the separation stops making sense.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers need to observe training and investigate unexpected results, but it does not state that solving a problem encountered during training requires understanding that problem beforehand.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that model research is very empirical. You have an idea, but whether it works—and whether it still works at a larger scale—depends on actually training the model. So training isn’t just executing a recipe that the research team hands over. It’s part of how you discover the recipe.

When a training run doesn’t behave as expected, you have to figure out whether the issue is the data, the architecture, the optimization, or the implementation. Those questions cross the boundary between research and engineering. If separate teams own each side, a lot of context can get lost in the handoff, and the feedback loop becomes slower.

You can certainly specialize within the team. But I think the people developing the ideas need to stay close to the training process and take responsibility for the results.

r001.rationale: The response says training issues must be diagnosed across research and engineering, but it does not say solving a problem encountered during training requires having understood that problem beforehand.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because the research and the training are tightly coupled. A research idea is usually based on assumptions about how the model will behave, but you only find out whether those assumptions are right when you actually train it. And the results of training determine what you should investigate next.

If you separate those into two teams, you create a handoff in the middle of that feedback loop. The training team might see something unexpected without knowing why a particular research decision was made, while the research team might miss details that are important for interpreting the result. You can divide responsibilities, of course, but the people doing research need to stay very close to the actual training.

r001.rationale: The response describes how training reveals whether research assumptions hold and why teams need a feedback loop. It does not state that solving a problem found during training requires understanding that problem beforehand.
